title: We're losing the ability to hold context and nuance
format: Talking head, nothing else (one take). Top title: NONE, only TikTok/IG native auto-captions (C10), exactly like @hoodsocialist #15. LONG VERSION: talking head 16:9 with black phrase cards on 'context collapse' and 'what's around this?' and the OECD and Marwick and boyd papers shown as receipts (2-3 s each).
hook: I don't think the problem is that people can't read anymore.

record.where: Bedroom, sitting on the edge of the bed, window light on your face, plain wall or curtain behind.
record.how: Your camera in landscape (16:9) on a stand at eye level, read from the teleprompter, same seat. Start mid-energy on the first word (no hello). Speak it like you are telling a friend something that has been bothering you.
record.wear: Something plain and dark so the face is the only thing to look at.

script:
### Open

I don't think the problem is that people can't read anymore. I think we are losing the ability to hold context and nuance.

People talk about how nobody can read anymore, nobody is smart anymore. But I don't think that's the whole problem. I think a lot of things are going on, and this is one of them.

### It's not just about being smart

When people say nobody can read anymore, I want to be fair. Some of it is true. The OECD measures adult reading skills across many countries, and in its latest survey, reading skills fell or stayed flat in most of them. So I'm not saying everything is fine.

*[on screen: OECD Survey of Adult Skills 2023, published December 2024]*

But I don't think intelligence is the whole story. Because I see very smart people, people who read very well, still miss the point of a conversation. And I think what they're missing is context.

### What holding context means

Holding context means you don't just look at what was said. You look at who said it, when they said it, who they said it to, and what they were replying to.

Think about a ten-second clip from a two-hour conversation. Or a screenshot of one tweet, without the thread around it. Or a quote where the sentence before it has been cut off. Every word in that clip can be true, and you can still walk away with the wrong meaning.

So holding context is the habit of asking, what's around this, before you decide what it means.

### What holding nuance means

The second thing we're losing is nuance, and it's very important to hold nuance. Holding nuance means being able to say, this is true, and that is also true, without feeling like you've lost the argument.

And conversations that concern us as humans are always so nuanced, because we are very complex. We are not just black and white. So when we lose the ability to hold nuance, we lose the ability to talk about people properly.

### Maybe I sound like a conspiracy theorist

Now, maybe I sound like a conspiracy theorist here. But I do think social media has a lot to do with this, and it turns out there's actually research on it.

Two researchers, Alice Marwick and danah boyd, called it context collapse. Online, what you say reaches lots of different people at once, and they read it without the setting you said it in.

*[on screen: Marwick and boyd (2011), New Media & Society]*

The apps are also built in a way that strips context out. Posts are short. Clips get cut out of long conversations, screenshots travel without the thread, and the feed rewards whoever reacts fastest. So we didn't suddenly become careless. We spend hours every day in places that cut things out of context.

### The "reading comprehension is dead" comments

And this one is funny. You've seen it in the comments. Someone says, reading comprehension is dead. But look at most of those arguments. The person usually read every single word correctly. What they missed was the joke, or the post before it, or who it was actually talking to.

So even the complaint that people can't read is often a context problem.

### Context is not an excuse

But I don't want to be unfair here, because context can be misused too. Holding context doesn't mean everything is fine once you know the background. Sometimes people say, you took it out of context, just to avoid owning something that really was wrong.

Holding context means looking at the whole thing. And sometimes, when you look at the whole thing, it's still bad. That's fine. At least now you're judging what actually happened.

### What the Bible says

There's a verse that says all of this in one line. Proverbs 18:13. "He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him." Answering before you've heard the whole thing is what reacting to a clip is.

### What I'm trying to do

So this is what I'm trying to do. Before I react, I ask, what's around this? I watch past the clip. I read the thread. And I try to ask what they meant before I ask what they said.

Do you find yourself reacting before you know the full story? Tell me in the comments.

script:
### Open

If I don't know something now, and I become aware that I don't know it, the very next thing is to close it. Boom. Search. Done.

And I feel like we've lost the art of not knowing. The art of just being okay with not knowing. I've been sitting with this for a while, so let me just think out loud about it.

I mean it in a few directions. There's the obvious one, not knowing what's going on in the world. We have access to everything now. You can know what happened everywhere on earth today, almost immediately, before you've even finished your breakfast. But I also mean it in the sense of just not knowing a thing. Not an event. Just a fact, a piece of knowledge, anything. And the more I think about it, the more I feel like it's the same thing underneath.

### We don't stay in not knowing

In reality, not knowing still exists. None of us knows everything, that hasn't changed. But in our actual conscious experience, not knowing has become a state we no longer stay in for very long. The not knowing barely gets to exist before it's gone.

### The gap

And I've been thinking about that gap specifically. The gap between realising you don't know something and actually knowing it. That gap used to be long. It could be days. You'd have to find a book, go to the library, or ask somebody, and they'd half-know, and they'd point you to somebody else. You might talk to three people about it. And sometimes, honestly, you would just never find out.

Now that gap is basically zero. And I think we've lost something that used to live inside that gap. I think it was curiosity.

Because there's a difference between being curious about something and just retrieving it. Curiosity is the state of having an open question. It's the wondering itself, the turning it over in your mind. And that state needs time. It needs the question to stay open long enough for you to actually sit inside it. If you close the question the second it appears, you never get to be curious. You just get to be informed.

### The gap was never empty

We treat that waiting time like it was dead time that technology kindly deleted for us. But things were happening in there. While the question stayed open, you'd carry it around with you. You'd guess. You'd come up with a theory and then throw it out. You'd notice things you wouldn't have noticed otherwise, because an open question makes you scan the world for pieces of the answer. And when you finally found it, days later, it landed somewhere. You'd built the room for it while you waited, and that's why it stayed.

And I wonder if that's why the things I look up in five seconds don't stick at all. The answer arrives and there's no room built for it. I look it up, and an hour later it's gone, and I look it up again. Because I never actually got curious about it. I just retrieved it.

There's a psychologist, George Loewenstein, who described curiosity as the feeling of a gap between what you know and what you want to know. When I read that, I was like, yeah. If there's no gap, there's no curiosity. So if you notice you're just not as curious about things as you used to be, I don't think there's anything wrong with you. I think the gap doesn't get to exist anymore.

*[on screen: George Loewenstein (1994), "The Psychology of Curiosity", Psychological Bulletin]*

### An opinion about everything

And then there's the other side of it, which is opinions. Everybody now has a take on everything, instantly. Every news story, every field, every country, every court case. And it makes sense, because you can look anything up in five, ten seconds and have a position. So there's no reason to ever say I don't know anymore. Not knowing is now technically a choice. People will literally say it to you, don't ask me stupid questions, ask Google.

But there is more that I don't know than there is that I do know. And that's practically true for every single person alive. Not knowing most things is everybody's normal state. We've just made it feel shameful.

### I'm not romanticising it

I don't want to be misunderstood here. I am not romanticising not knowing. I have spent my whole life being someone who wants to know things. Access to information is genuinely one of the best things we have, and I am not going to pretend ignorance is better. I do not want to go back to a time where a question just sits unanswered for months because nobody around me happened to know the answer. And there's a version of not knowing that's just outright laziness, and I'm not talking about that either.

What I'm talking about is that prolonged state of not knowing, the one that used to come before you finally knew. I feel like we've lost it, and I think it was doing something for us. It powers curiosity in a unique way.

There's that old line, iron sharpens iron. It's friction that does it. And I think the open question was a kind of friction. It rubbed against you while it stayed open, and something got sharpened.

### Close

So I'm learning to be comfortable with not knowing sometimes. On purpose. Just, oh, I don't know, tell me about it. And leaving it there for a bit. I'll still look it up eventually, I'm not going to pretend I won't. But I'm letting the gap stay open a little longer before I rush to close it.

I have a feeling the wondering was the good part. I don't know. I'm still thinking about it.

When was the last time you let a question stay open? Tell me in the comments.

script:
### Open

Someone says, I like rice. And another person in the comment section replies, why do you hate beans? Nobody said anything about beans.

I don't have the perfect words for this. But there's something I like to describe as the binary classification of knowledge, and social media promotes it. If you use social media a lot, you've probably started thinking in binary, whether you meant to or not. You think in two ways. Good or bad, for or against, with me or against me. In a binary mind, liking one thing means you must be against the other. And honestly, I don't find it surprising at all.

### The buttons

At its root, social media is algorithms. Computer programs. And computers run on binary, ones and zeros. Maybe I'm blabbing here. But the more I think about it, the less I think it's the ones and zeros. I think it's the buttons.

Look at what the apps actually let you do. You like a post or you don't. You follow or unfollow, upvote or downvote, keep scrolling or stop. Almost every choice the app gives you has two sides, and you make those choices hundreds of times a day. So you're practising binary judgement over and over, without even noticing.

I study human-computer interaction, and one idea I keep running into is that the tools we use shape the way we think. There's an old line people usually credit to Marshall McLuhan, but it was actually his friend John Culkin who wrote it. "We shape our tools, and thereafter our tools shape us." I think that's what's happening to us. We were given a thumbs up and a thumbs down for everything, and slowly we started looking at the whole world that way.

*[on screen: John Culkin, "A Schoolman's Guide to Marshall McLuhan", Saturday Review, 1967]*

### Why it's so easy

Our brains don't mind binary thinking, honestly. Two boxes are easy. Putting something in a box is quick, and it feels like clarity. "It depends" is slow, and "it's a bit of both" is uncomfortable. When you're scrolling fast, and everyone around you is reacting fast, you don't have time for slow, so the quick box wins.

Psychologists even have a name for it when it gets serious. All-or-nothing thinking, or black-and-white thinking. It's the kind of thinking where one mistake means you're a failure, one bad day means the whole week is ruined, and one wrong opinion means a person is completely bad.

### How we write now

What convinced me that social media is changing how heavy users think is how people write now. People write defensively before anybody has even replied. I like rice, no shade to beans. Not to say this other thing is bad, but. We add disclaimers to our own preferences, because we already expect to be read in two ways. So we're not only reading other people that way. We're writing for an audience we expect to read us that way.

### How it spreads

And once binary thinking gets inside you, it spreads. Opinions start coming in packages. If you believe this, you must also believe that. You can't disagree with a friend on one thing without it feeling like you're against them. You can't criticise something you love, because in two boxes, criticism means you hate it.

And the hardest part is when we start doing it to ourselves. I'm either succeeding or I'm failing. I'm either a good person or a bad one. There's no room for, I'm growing, I'm learning, I'm better than I was and I'm not where I want to be yet.

Most of real life happens between the two boxes. A person who was wrong then and is right now. Two things that are true at the same time. Relationships, faith, people. Most of the important things in life are not ones and zeros.

### The fair part

Now, let me be fair. Some things really are binary. A fact is true, or it isn't. Consent is yes, or no. Right and wrong are real. So I'm not saying everything is grey and nothing can be judged. Two boxes are fine for the things that really come in two. The trouble starts when we force two boxes onto things that come in many shades, and the skill is knowing which one you're looking at.

### Faith

And this is where Jesus fascinates me. Jesus wasn't afraid of a real binary. He said, let your yes be yes, and your no be no. But when people handed him a false one, he refused it.

His disciples once saw a man who was born blind, and they asked him, who sinned, this man or his parents? Two options. And Jesus said, neither. Then he said this happened so that the works of God would be shown in him. That answer wasn't on their list at all.

Another time, people tried to trap him with a yes or no question. Should we pay taxes to Caesar, or not? And he said, give to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and give to God what belongs to God. Again and again, he stepped out of the boxes people built for him.

*[on screen: Matthew 5:37, John 9:1-3, Matthew 22:21]*

### Close

So this is what I'm trying to practise. When I feel myself reaching for one of two boxes, I stop and ask, is this actually a two-box thing? Most of the time, it isn't. You can like rice and like beans. You can love something and still see what's wrong with it. You can disagree with someone and still be for them.

What's something you've seen people put in two boxes that doesn't belong there? Tell me in the comments.

title: A rule of thumb for complimenting strangers

script:
### Open

There's a rule of thumb for complimenting people, especially strangers. I read it somewhere, and I've been thinking about it since, so let me pass it on. Compliment something they were intentional about. Something they had control over, an actual, active choice that they made.

### The rule

So for example, somebody has new braids. You can say, oh my God, I love your braids, because they went out of their way to make that hair. Somebody's necklace, their earrings, their rings. The way they smell, I love your perfume. Their piercings. Something creative they've done with their appearance, their shirt, their tie, their jacket, their bag, their shoes. They dyed their hair a new colour. Their music taste. All of that is fair game, and all of it is safe.

What you're avoiding is the opposite. The shape of their head. The length of their legs. Things they did not choose and cannot change. Except of course there are exceptions to the rule.

### Why it works

And I want to explain why this rule works, because when I sat with it, it's actually deeper than just manners.

When you compliment somebody's choice, you're complimenting their mind. That jacket was a decision. Those braids were hours in a chair. That perfume was somebody standing in a shop, smelling things, thinking, is this me? Every one of those is a person who stood in front of a mirror, made a decision and hoped it would land. So when you say I love your braids, what you're actually telling them is, the thing you were hoping for happened. Somebody noticed. It costs you nothing, and it lands directly.

If you compliment something a person didn't choose, they can't really receive it. There's nothing to accept, because they didn't do anything. They just have to stand there while you assess them. It also tells them you've been studying their body, which is a whole different feeling. And if you can rank them up, you can rank them down. A compliment about something they can't change tells them they're on a scale in your head. That's why those ones land cold, even when they were meant warmly.

And let's be honest about the stranger part especially. For a woman, a comment about her body from a man she doesn't know can make her want to leave. A comment about her boots is just a nice moment. Same intention, completely different result.

### What the research says

Now let me tell you what I found that shocked me a little. Two researchers, Erica Boothby and Vanessa Bohns, ran five studies asking why people don't give more compliments. They found that we keep underestimating how good the other person will feel, and we overestimate how bothered and uncomfortable they'll be.

*[on screen: Boothby and Bohns (2021), Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin]*

And the wrong prediction was coming from the giver's own anxiety. Our own worry about whether we'll sound weird, whether we'll do it right. When they had other people watch the same moment and predict how it would go, those people got it right. So the awkwardness is inside your head, and it's about you, not about them. And the people who gave the compliments felt better afterwards, despite the dread going in.

So basically we are all walking around holding kind words hostage because of a fear the research says isn't real.

### There are levels to it

There are levels to it, though. The choices are the safe ground, always available. Then there are things that aren't chosen exactly but are still done, like somebody's laugh, or their smile, or the energy they bring into a room.

And then there's the highest level, which is complimenting somebody's character. You were so patient with that woman at the counter. You explained that so clearly. Those ones follow people home. They're harder with strangers, because you need to have actually watched something, but when you can, please do.

The Bible has this line I love. "A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver." The right words at the right time are worth something.

### Why I'm talking about this

I've been receiving a lot of compliments here since I got to Estonia. And I want to be more intentional about giving compliments as well.

You are probably going to think something nice about a stranger today. Their bag, their hair, their shoes, something. So say it. It costs you two seconds and one small moment of feeling silly.

Compliment what they chose. What's the best compliment a stranger ever gave you? Tell me in the comments. Rule of thumb. Thank me later.

script:
### Open

I absolutely cannot stand it when people police reading.

Oh, I don't respect people who read fiction. Oh, people who read self-help are not serious. Oh, if you read romance you're not really reading. Oh, ebooks don't count. Oh, audiobooks? That's not reading, you're just listening. Everybody has become a reading referee all of a sudden. And I'm looking at all of you like, since when? Since when did we, of all people, earn the right to police reading this much?

### We don't even read that much

Because let's be real about the actual numbers. In the US, depending on which survey you check, somewhere between a quarter and nearly half of adults did not read a single book in the past year. Not one. A YouGov survey at the end of 2025 found forty percent of Americans didn't finish one book all year, and of the people who did read, the median was two books. Two, for the whole year. And reading for pleasure on an average day has been falling for two decades.

*[on screen: Pew Research Center 2021: 23% read no book; YouGov December 2025: 40%, median 2 books; American Time Use Survey]*

So this is the field we are standing on. Most people are not reading much at all. And in the middle of that, a small handful of people who do read have somehow decided that their real job is to stand at the door and rank everybody else's choices.

It's like being in a town where almost nobody exercises, and the three people who go to the gym are standing in the corner arguing about whether the treadmill is real cardio. My brother. My sister. Nobody is exercising. Sit down.

### It's never the big readers

And have you noticed it's never actually the big readers doing this? The people who genuinely read a lot, who read wide, are the most relaxed people about it. They'll read a novel, then a biography, then a book about mushrooms, then the back of a cereal box. They're not out here gatekeeping, because they actually love the thing.

"I'm the type of person who looks down on self-help" is a very cheap sentence to say. It costs you nothing. It's a personality you can wear without reading a single page. Actually reading forty books a year is expensive. It costs time and attention. So people buy the look of the reader instead, and the look comes with a nose you can look down.

### The rules contradict each other

And this is what gives the whole game away. The rules contradict each other completely. If you read fiction, they say you're escaping reality, you're not reading anything useful. Okay, so you read non-fiction instead, and now they say you're joyless, you only read to optimise yourself. You read something literary and difficult, you're a snob. You read something fun and easy, you're not a serious reader. There is literally no book you can pick up that somebody won't have a problem with. And when every possible choice is wrong, the books were never the point. It was about having something to feel superior about.

### The ones that get bullied the most

Let me defend the ones that get bullied the most. Self-help gets the most sneering, right? But what is self-help usually? It's a person trying to be better. Trying to manage their money, trying to be less anxious, trying to heal something, trying to fix a habit that's hurting them. Since when is a human being trying to improve their own life something to be embarrassed about?

Romance is one of the most mocked genres and also one of the best-selling, which is already funny. It's mostly women reading about being wanted and safe and chosen, and I'll let you sit with why that genre gets that much mockery.

And the audiobook thing, let me just kill it, because people say it with so much confidence. Listening isn't really reading. Actually, the research says understanding a book by reading it and by listening to it is broadly the same for most material. Your brain gets to the meaning either way. So the single mother listening to a book on her commute, because that's the only twenty minutes she has, is reading. Full stop. She's doing better than the person who read zero books this year but has strong opinions about her format.

### Cooking books

Me, personally? I want to read cooking books. I don't care. That is the most harmless thing in the entire world, and I promise you somebody would still find a way to have an opinion about it.

### Close

Reading is one of the few good, cheap, quiet habits we have left, and it's fighting a thousand louder, faster things for the same little pockets of your time. And instead of being glad that anybody at all is still turning pages, some readers spend their energy making the door smaller. Every time you make somebody feel stupid for how they read or what they read, you don't create a better reader. You create one more person who decides reading is not for them.

So please. Physical book, ebook, audiobook, whichever one you prefer. Fiction, non-fiction, self-help, romance, cookbooks, whatever gets you turning the page. We are too much of non-readers for us to be policing reading this much. Just read. Just freaking read, man.

What's a book you've been made to feel bad for reading? Tell me in the comments.

script:
### Open

I think the internet did so well that we now know more people than we should know. We have more access to information than we should have. And I don't think we've ever really sat down to process that.

### 1991

In 1991, something very interesting happened to humanity. The World Wide Web went public. The internet existed before then in some form, but 1991 is when it stopped being something only institutions used and became something an ordinary person could open. You, me, anybody with a connection.

Before that, we were limited in several ways. The people you knew were limited, basically to whoever was physically near you. The knowledge you had access to was limited to whatever books reached your town and whatever the people around you happened to know. Your circle of influence was significantly limited.

Then the internet happened, and all of a sudden there are billions of people I can reach from my phone. I can open this thing in my hand and reach more people than all my ancestors could reach combined. And it is a good thing. I want to say that clearly, because I mean it, and I'll come back to it. Look at how much has changed in the world since then. It was evolutionary.

### What I mean by "should"

When I say we know more people than we should, I don't mean "should" in a moral way. I'm not saying there's forbidden knowledge, and I'm not saying go back to the village. What I mean is closer to this. A human being should not drink forty litres of water. Water isn't bad. The body that processes it was just never built for that much. It's a capacity problem.

### About 150 people

And there's an actual number for this. There's an anthropologist called Robin Dunbar who studied primates, and he found that the size of the social group a species can hold matches the size of a particular part of their brain. So he ran the numbers for humans, and the answer he got is about 150.

*[on screen: Dunbar's number, about 150 (Robin Dunbar, 1992)]*

You can keep real relationships with about 150 people. And by real I mean you actually know them, you know your history with them, and you know how they connect to everybody else. And it comes in layers. About five people in your innermost circle, the ones you'd call at 2am. Around fifteen close friends. About fifty. Then 150. Then about 500 acquaintances, and about 1,500 faces you can simply recognise.

*[on screen: rings of 5, 15, 50, 150, 500 and 1,500]*

People argue about the exact number, and it changes from person to person, so think of it as somewhere between 100 and 200. But it keeps showing up, in hunter-gatherer groups, in villages and in army units.

Dunbar was asked about social media, and his answer was basically that when people have thousands of followers, those extra people are not new friends. They're your outer layers filling up. So the technology gave you a lot more people to see, and your capacity stayed the same. Your brain still has about 150 seats, and now there are millions of people standing in the room.

### People who don't know you exist

So what happens to everybody who doesn't get a seat? Your brain does not have a setting that says this person is content, not a human being. Two researchers, Donald Horton and Richard Wohl, named this in 1956, just from watching people with radio and television. They called it parasocial interaction. It's the feeling of a real relationship with somebody who does not know you exist.

*[on screen: Horton and Wohl (1956), Psychiatry]*

And you see it. You see how people grieve when a creator they've never met stops posting. You see how betrayed people feel when someone they've never spoken to changes their opinion on something. I don't think that's stupidity. I think that's a 150-seat brain doing what it was built to do, in a place it was never built for.

### Knowing more than you can do

And it's the same with information. For most of human history, what you could know about suffering was about the same size as what you could do about it. You heard the child was sick because the child lived down your street, and you could carry food down that street.

Now, before you've even brushed your teeth, you can know about a war, a flood and a building that collapsed, on different continents. And you can do almost nothing about any of it. So when people say they feel numb, or tired, or guilty for scrolling past something terrible, I don't think they've stopped caring. They have one body, one salary and one afternoon.

### The fair part

Now let me be fair, because I mean this. The people who gained the most from the internet are the people who were furthest from power. Access used to depend on where you were born. A brilliant person in the wrong town simply never got to find out what they could have been. The internet changed that, and it changed it most for people like us. *[your line, optional: one sentence about what the internet made possible for you.]*

So the internet was not a mistake. Our access multiplied by billions, and our capacity stayed the same, and I don't think we've ever acknowledged that gap.

### Close

I'm not logging off, and I don't think you are either. But every generation before us had their limits set for them. Geography decided who you knew. Distance decided what you heard about. We are the first people who have to choose our own limits, on purpose, on apps built to keep giving us more.

So if you feel like your head is too full, like you know too much and can do too little, I don't think there's anything wrong with you. Figuring out what to let in used to be geography's job. Now it's ours.

How do you decide who and what gets a seat in your head? Tell me in the comments.

script:
### Open

Life moves on is such a literal phrase, in all ramifications.

Because life actually moves on. You think you're still overwhelmed by the trials and the demands and the remnants of yesterday, and before you even blink your eyes properly to take that in, today pops in with its own fresh deliveries o. Fresh ones. Nobody asked you if you were ready. Nobody checked whether you finished unpacking yesterday's own.

### The other face of the phrase

Normally we offer the phrase as comfort. Somebody is going through something and we tell them, don't worry, life moves on, and what we mean is the pain will pass, time will do its healing thing. Which is true. But take the phrase literally for one second and you'll see its other face. Life moves on means life does not wait. It just moves, whether you have processed anything or not. You're still standing in the middle of yesterday's scattered boxes and the doorbell is ringing again. Today has arrived, and today came with its own full load.

### The courier

I started thinking of every morning like a delivery you never ordered and cannot refuse. There's no "sorry we missed you" slip. No rescheduling. No return address to send it back to. You open your eyes and the package is already on the doorstep. Life is honestly the only courier with a perfect delivery record. Rain, grief, public holiday, it does not matter, the van still comes.

Anyone who has lost something big knows how strange this feels. The world just continues. Buses still run. People are laughing in cafes like nothing happened. Your inbox is still filling up. You almost want the whole world to observe one minute of silence for your situation, and the world simply will not do it. But it's also true in the small everyday version. You didn't even finish being tired from yesterday, you haven't concluded yesterday's matter in your head, and today is already presenting its own agenda.

### Each day has enough trouble of its own

Now, this could easily become a depressing observation, so let me tell you why it isn't, at least not for me. Jesus made this exact point, and I find it so funny that we quote it all the time without noticing how literal he was being. Matthew 6. Do not worry about tomorrow, tomorrow will worry about itself, each day has enough trouble of its own. Each day has enough trouble of its own! The days come pre-loaded. That is simply the design. And that is exactly why the instruction is one day at a time. It's rationing. One day's delivery per day is what your back was built to carry. Most of our overwhelm, if you check it, is us carrying three days at once. Yesterday's remnants, today's fresh one, plus tomorrow's own that hasn't even shipped yet, and we've already collected it in our imagination.

*[on screen: Matthew 6:34]*

### New every morning

And there's one more thing about this courier that changes everything for me. The book of Lamentations, of all places, a book written from inside actual rubble, says his mercies are new every morning. New every morning. Same delivery schedule as the trouble. So it's two packages on the same doorstep, every single day, and both of them are fresh. The door that keeps opening to admit new demands is the same door admitting new grace. Life refusing to pause is annoying until you realise it's also life refusing to leave you behind.

*[on screen: Lamentations 3:22-23]*

### Close

So no, you cannot stop the deliveries. They will keep coming, that one is settled, it's not in your hands. What is in your hands is which package you sign for first each morning, and whether you learn to actually close a day. Finish it. Unpack what you can, thank God for what went well, hand over what you couldn't resolve, and let the day end. Because the van is coming again tomorrow. It always comes. And so does the mercy.

How do you close a day? Tell me in the comments.

script:
### Open

Creating imaginary school fees for your struggling parents should be a crime.

I think there are some things that are not explicitly crimes. They're not crimes, nobody will arrest you for them, but I genuinely think they qualify. There should be some kind of review where certain behaviours are examined and upgraded to criminal activity. So I'm starting a list. Things that should be crimes. And episode one is for my Nigerian students, past and present, because you people know what you did.

### The crime

Why are you, a child of struggling parents, parents that are sending you to university by force by fire, and if you know Nigeria you know that is not a cheap thing, it is not easy to send a child to university, why are you, that same child, sitting down in your hostel inventing fees?

Your parents are already struggling to meet up with the real obligations. The actual school fees. The hostel rent. The dues that genuinely exist. Your feeding. They are stretching themselves to cover the real cost of you being in that school. And then you, the child of struggling parents, decide that you need more things. Clothes, cool stuff, enjoyment. Which, fine, you're young, you want things, that part is human. But instead of asking honestly, you take it upon yourself to create imaginary bills. Faculty handbook fee. Departmental levy. Practical manual money. Course rep said we're contributing for the lecturer's birthday. You are creating expenses that do not exist and sending them to two people who cannot afford the ones that do exist. You build more struggles onto the original struggles of you being in school, with your full chest. How is that not a crime?

### It actually is a crime

And this is the part that made me laugh when I thought about it properly. It is a crime. Technically, legally, what I just described is obtaining money by false pretences. That is fraud. That is literally the same 419 we shout about in this country. Inventing a fee that doesn't exist and collecting money for it is the textbook definition.

*[on screen: Section 419, Criminal Code Act (Nigeria): obtaining by false pretences]*

So this behaviour is already in the law books. It is just the only crime with no prosecutions, because the victims are the only two people on this earth who would never report you. The scheme works because their love for you is the security flaw.

### Where the money came from

Now let me spoil the joke, because the joke deserves to be spoiled. A struggling parent does not have a miscellaneous section in their budget. So your fake fifteen thousand naira levy did not come from savings. It's your mother re-tying the same two wrappers for another year. It's your father postponing that hospital check he has been mentioning. It's meat leaving the pot at home while you're buying shawarma on campus with the proceeds of your fraud. You taxed people who were already taxing themselves for you.

### Why it happens

I know why it happens though, and I'll be honest about it, because I want this to be fair and not just a dragging session. Campus runs on a lot of pressure to look like you have money. Nobody wants to be the visibly poor one. The pressure to have the clothes, to contribute when the group is contributing, to belong, it's real. So most of the time it wasn't even greed. It was shame, sending its bill to the people least able to pay it. You were trying to hide the family's struggle at school by increasing the family's struggle at home. When you say it like that, you can see the maths doesn't even make sense.

### The Bible saw you coming

And in case anybody wants to do the classic excuse, it's not really stealing, it's my parents, it's still family money, the Bible saw you coming from thousands of years away. Proverbs 28 says whoever robs their father or their mother and says it is no sin is partner to a destroyer. Partner to a destroyer o. The excuse itself is quoted in the verse.

*[on screen: Proverbs 28:24]*

### What now

So where does this leave us? If you're grown now, earning now, and your parents still don't know about the lab coat levy of your second year, the restitution process is simple. It's called taking care of them now, generously, with interest. Pay back the fraud in kindness.

And let me tell you the part that will actually touch you. Some of those parents knew. The fee sounded strange, the amounts kept coming, they looked at the numbers and something didn't add up, and they paid anyway. Because what if this one is real? What if they doubt you and you suffer at school because of their doubt? They would rather be cheated than risk failing you. So for some of you, the crime was forgiven before you even collected the money.

### Close

Episode one, closed. The list continues. If you have a nomination for something that should be a crime, drop it in the comments, because I know you people are holding evidence.

script:
### Open

How does a website check your password if it doesn't store your password? Because a well-built website does not keep your password. I'm a software developer, and I'm going to show you what it keeps instead, with one example password the whole way through.

### The example

Say you sign up to a website with the password jollof123. Please don't use that password, it's just our example. You press sign up, and your password travels to the website's server. If the website is well built, the first thing the server does is make sure jollof123 never gets saved anywhere.

*[on screen: password: jollof123]*

### What a hash is

It runs your password through something called a hash function. A hash function is a bit of maths that takes any text and turns it into a long jumble of characters. Two things make it useful. The same input always gives the same jumble. And it only works one way. You can turn jollof123 into the jumble, but you can't turn the jumble back into jollof123.

*[on screen: jollof123, an arrow, then a long jumble like $2y$12$Kx9...]*

So the website saves the jumble in its database, and your actual password is never written down.

### What a salt is

But there's a problem. Lots of people use the same simple passwords. If everyone with jollof123 got the same jumble, an attacker could build a big list of common passwords and their jumbles in advance, and just look yours up.

So before hashing, the website adds a salt. A salt is a random string, different for every user. Even if you and I both use jollof123, my salt and your salt are different, so our jumbles come out completely different. The salt isn't a secret. It's saved right next to the jumble. Its job is to make every user's jumble unique, so a list made in advance is useless.

*[on screen: two rows. jollof123 + salt A gives jumble A. jollof123 + salt B gives jumble B.]*

### What happens when you log in

Now you come back and log in. You type jollof123 again. The server takes your saved salt, adds it to what you just typed, and runs it through the same hash function. Then it compares the new jumble with the one in the database. If they match, you typed the right password, and you're in. If even one character is different, the jumble is completely different, and you're not.

So the website checked your password without ever keeping it.

### Slow on purpose

One more thing. The hash functions made for passwords, like bcrypt or Argon2, are slow on purpose. You don't notice it, because checking one password takes a fraction of a second. But if someone steals the database and tries to guess billions of passwords, that slowness adds up very fast. That's the point.

In Laravel, which is what I use at work, this is built in. When you call Hash::make, it uses bcrypt by default and handles the salt for you. And Hash::check does the comparing when someone logs in.

*[on screen: Hash::make($password) and Hash::check($typed, $savedHash)]*

### What this means for you

This is why forgot password sends you a link to make a new password. The website can't send you your old one, because it doesn't have it. And if a website ever emails you your actual password, that's a red flag. It means they stored it in a way they can read.

Hashing doesn't save a weak password, though. If your password is jollof123, an attacker with a stolen database will try common passwords first, and they'll find it. And if you use the same password everywhere, one leaked site can unlock the rest, because attackers try leaked emails and passwords on other sites. So use a long password, use a different one for every site, and let a password manager remember them for you.

### Close

So the next time you log in, the website is comparing a jumble with a jumble. Did you know websites don't keep your password? Tell me in the comments.

script:
### Open

When you pay online with your card, your payment passes through at least four different companies in a few seconds. So what actually happens between you pressing pay and seeing payment successful? Let's follow one payment all the way through.

### The example

Say you're buying a dress for fifteen thousand naira from an online store, and the store uses Paystack. You add it to your cart, go to checkout, type in your card number, the expiry date and the three numbers at the back, and press pay.

### The payment gateway

Your card details don't go to the store. They go to Paystack. Paystack is a payment gateway, the middleman between the store and the banks. The store never has to touch your card number, which is one reason small stores use a gateway instead of building all of this themselves.

*[on screen: four boxes in a row: STORE, PAYSTACK, CARD NETWORK, YOUR BANK]*

### The card network

Paystack then sends the request through the card network. That's the company whose logo is on your card, Visa, Mastercard or Verve, which is the Nigerian one. The card network's job is to carry the message to the right bank, and your card number tells it which bank issued your card.

### Your bank

Now your bank, the bank that issued your card, checks two things. Is this really you? And do you have fifteen thousand naira? To check that it's really you, your bank sends an OTP to your phone, a one-time password, or asks for your PIN. That extra step is how banks stop someone who has only stolen your card number.

If you pass both, your bank says approved, and it holds the fifteen thousand naira on your account.

### The way back

The answer travels back the same way. Your bank tells the card network, the card network tells Paystack, Paystack tells the store, and your screen says payment successful. All of that happens in a few seconds.

Paystack also sends the store's server a separate message in the background to say this payment succeeded. Developers call that a webhook. It's how the store knows to send your dress even if you closed the tab before the page loaded.

### When the store actually gets paid

But the store doesn't get the money in that moment. Approved means the money is promised. The actual money moves later, between the banks, in batches. That part is called settlement. Paystack pays businesses in Nigeria the next working day.

*[on screen: Paystack Nigeria: settlement the next working day (T+1), paystack.com/pricing]*

And the store doesn't get the full fifteen thousand. Paystack takes a fee. For local payments in Nigeria, it's 1.5 percent plus 100 naira, capped at 2,000 naira. On fifteen thousand naira, that's 325 naira, so the store gets 14,675 naira.

*[on screen: 1.5% of 15,000 = 225, plus 100 = 325 naira fee]*

### When it fails

This is also why payments fail sometimes. Any of these steps can say no. Your bank can decline because the payment looks unusual, or because your card isn't enabled for online payments. Or the connection can time out on the way back. That's how you sometimes get debited while the store says the payment failed. Your bank held the money, but the approval never made it back. Usually the bank reverses it.

And if you pay with Google Pay, which Paystack added for Nigerian businesses in September, the path is the same. Your phone just sends a stand-in number called a token instead of your real card number.

### Close

So when you press pay, at least four companies talk to each other in a few seconds: the store, Paystack, the card network and your bank. And the store gets the money the next working day. Have you ever been debited for a payment that failed? Tell me what happened in the comments.

title: CORS explained: why the browser blocks your request
format: Her on camera, 16:9, with the browser behind her (TV/slide-behind format): frame 1 is the red CORS error in a browser console (generic mock), then her explaining with the graphics cut in (style from @kodekloud: handwritten 'CORS' title, a yellow mark on ORIGIN, then PREFLIGHT, then the header name). hook: What is CORS, and why is it blocking your request?

record.how: Normal pace (not the fast short pace), your camera in landscape (16:9). Sitting, a little faster than usual so it fits under a minute, still clear. Say 'localhost three thousand' and 'localhost eight thousand'.

script:
### Open

What is CORS, and why is it blocking your request? If you've built a frontend that talks to an API, you've probably seen this red error in the console. I'll explain it with one example the whole way through.

*[on screen: the console error: Access to fetch at 'http://localhost:8000/api/books' from origin 'http://localhost:3000' has been blocked by CORS policy]*

### The example

Say your frontend runs on localhost three thousand, and your API runs on localhost eight thousand. Your frontend calls the API to get a list of books. You open the browser, and instead of books, you get a CORS error. But when you test the same API in Postman, it works. So what's going on?

### What an origin is

To the browser, those two are different origins. An origin is three things together. The protocol, like http or https. The domain, like localhost. And the port, like three thousand. If any one of the three is different, it's a different origin. Here the protocol and the domain are the same, but the port is different, so the browser treats your frontend and your API like two different websites.

*[on screen: http + localhost + 3000 next to http + localhost + 8000, the port circled]*

### The same-origin policy

By default, the browser doesn't let a page read a response from another origin. That's called the same-origin policy, and it's there to protect you. Imagine you're logged into your bank in one tab, and you open some random website in another tab. Without this rule, that random website could send a request to your bank, with your login cookies, and read your account details. The same-origin policy stops that.

And this is what confuses a lot of people. Often the request did reach your API, and your server even answered. The browser just refuses to hand the answer to your JavaScript. That's also why Postman works. Postman isn't a browser, so it doesn't apply this rule.

### What CORS is

CORS stands for Cross-Origin Resource Sharing. It's how a server tells the browser, I trust this other origin, you can let it read my responses. The server does it with a header. Your API sends back Access-Control-Allow-Origin, with http://localhost:3000 in it. The browser sees that header, sees that it matches the page, and lets your JavaScript have the books.

*[on screen: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:3000]*

### The preflight

Sometimes the browser asks first. If your request sends JSON, or an Authorization header, or uses a method like PUT or DELETE, the browser sends a small request before the real one. It's called a preflight, and it uses the OPTIONS method. It's the browser asking the server, is this origin allowed to send this kind of request? If the server answers yes with the right headers, the real request goes. If the server doesn't handle OPTIONS, you get a CORS error even though your real route works fine.

*[on screen: OPTIONS /api/books, then the real GET]*

### The fix is on the server

So the real fix is on the server, because only the server can say who it trusts. In Laravel, CORS is handled for you by middleware, and the settings live in config/cors.php. If you don't see that file, you can publish it with php artisan config:publish cors. Then you put your frontend's origin in allowed_origins.

*[on screen: 'allowed_origins' => ['http://localhost:3000']*

]

When you deploy, you add your real frontend address there too, like https://yourapp.com.

### The star

You'll see people online say, just put a star and allow every origin. That can be fine for a public API with no login. But if your frontend sends cookies or credentials, the browser won't accept the star. It needs the exact origin, and in Laravel you also turn on supports_credentials. And allowing every origin on an API with logins is exactly the thing the same-origin policy was protecting you from.

### Close

So when you see a CORS error, your API is usually fine. The browser is protecting the user, and your server needs to tell it who to trust. What's the error that confused you the most when you started coding? Tell me in the comments.

script:
### Open

Google Wallet is now in Nigeria, but your card might not work with it. Google announced it on Wednesday, the 28th of October, so you can now pay by tapping your Android phone in a shop.

*[on screen: Techpoint Africa, 28 October 2026]*

### What it is

Google Wallet is the app on Android phones that holds your cards. Once your card is in it, you hold your phone near a card machine to pay, the same way you'd tap a contactless card. You can also use it to pay in apps and online, where it's called Google Pay. And it can hold things like boarding passes, event tickets and loyalty cards.

### Which cards work

But not every card works yet. Right now, Google's list is mostly Mastercard. FirstBank Mastercard debit cards. GTBank Mastercard debit and prepaid cards. Zenith Bank Mastercard credit, debit and prepaid cards. And UBA Mastercard cards, plus UBA's Visa prepaid card, which is the only Visa card on the list.

*[on screen: Google's list: FirstBank, GTBank, Zenith Bank, UBA]*

Visa said Visa cardholders in Nigeria can now use Google Pay, but Google's own list is narrower. Verve isn't on it, and that matters, because Verve is the card a lot of Nigerians carry. Statista data, cited by Techpoint, says Verve was 54 percent of the cards used for POS and online payments between 2019 and 2022. Cards from OPay, Moniepoint, Kuda and PalmPay aren't on the list either.

### What you need

To tap and pay, you need an Android phone with NFC. NFC is the chip that lets your phone talk to a card machine when you hold it close. Malik Asamu, the CEO of CashAfrica, told Techpoint that about half of Android phones in Nigeria have it. You also confirm each payment on your phone with your fingerprint, your face or your PIN.

And the shop's POS has to accept contactless. A lot of POS machines in Nigeria don't have the hardware for that, and the shop has to pay to upgrade.

### Is it safe?

When you tap, your phone doesn't send the shop your real card number. It sends a stand-in number called a token, so if the shop's system is ever hacked, your real card number isn't there. In Nigeria, Interswitch built the part that connects the banks and creates those tokens, together with Mastercard.

The Central Bank also set contactless limits in 2023, fifteen thousand naira per payment and fifty thousand naira a day without a PIN or a fingerprint. The banks haven't said yet how those limits apply to Google Pay.

### Paying online

Online, you may have seen it already. Paystack turned on Google Pay at checkout for Nigerian businesses in September. But you only see it where the business has switched it on, and where your card and your phone are supported.

*[your reaction: one or two sentences in your own words. Would you use it? We have not written this for you.]*

### Close

CashAfrica estimates that contactless is about 0.1 percent of payments in Nigeria right now. So my honest question is, how many POS machines around you will actually take a phone tap? Have you tried it yet? Tell me in the comments.

title: AI companies agree on one way to say 'don't train on my site'
format: Talking head + receipt (@funmiyakubu #12). Top title: white rounded box, black heavy lowercase (T3): 'one line to stop AI training on your site'. script:
### Open

Soon, one line on your website could tell OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic not to train their AI on it. All four have said they'll respect the same signal.

*[on screen: OpenAI, "Helping websites express AI training preferences", 30 October 2026]*

### What robots.txt is

Every website can have a small public file called robots.txt. You can see it on most sites by typing the site's address, then slash robots.txt. It tells the bots that visit the site which pages they can and can't crawl. Search engines have respected it for about thirty years.

*[on screen: a generic robots.txt file]*

### How it worked until now

Until now, if you didn't want AI companies training on your site, you had to block each company's bot one by one, by name. And you had to keep up with new bots as they appeared.

### The new line

The new idea is one line that all of them honour. It's a token called usage AI training. In your robots.txt you write User-Agent, then that token, then Disallow, slash. That says, don't use anything on this site to train generative AI. You can still add Allow lines for pages you're happy to share.

*[on screen: User-Agent: __usage_ai-training, then Disallow: /]*

And it controls training, not crawling. Microsoft says Bing search listings will not be affected.

### Who's in, and when

It's a proposal written by Kevin Kelley, Anthropic's standards lead, for the IETF, the group that writes a lot of the internet's rules. It was filed on the 30th of October as an individual draft, which means it's not an official standard yet.

Anthropic says it has already started supporting it. Microsoft says the 1st of February 2027. Google says 2027. OpenAI says in the coming months. And Meta called a shared signal an important step, but it didn't say whether it will honour it.

*[on screen: a simple table of the five companies and their dates]*

### What it doesn't do

It's voluntary, so it only works on companies that choose to follow it. It doesn't take back anything that has already been used for training. And it doesn't settle the bigger questions about copyright, or paying the people whose work was used.

*[your reaction, optional: one or two sentences, your own view as a developer and someone who writes online. We have not written this for you.]*

script:
### Open

Since I started my master's in Estonia, I've written only one exam, and we were allowed to use ChatGPT in it.

Honestly, I wouldn't even call it an exam in the Nigerian sense. We were allowed to use our phone, our laptop, the internet, even ChatGPT.

Imagine you're in Nigeria and you're caught with your phone in an exam. Expulsion. Carry-over at the minimum.

### Why it works here

But it works here because the questions are not asking you to reproduce information. They're not asking you to memorise a definition and write it back. They're asking you to apply knowledge to a problem. So even if you Google the concept, if you don't understand it well enough to use it, having your phone wouldn't help you. And honestly, I think it's harder in some way, because you cannot just cram the night before.

### In Nigeria, the exam decides

How you're assessed is also different between Nigeria and Europe. In a lot of Nigerian universities, the final exam carries most of your grade. Sometimes the final exam is 70 percent of your grade, and your continuous assessment is maybe 30 percent.

*[on screen: University of Nigeria, Nsukka (example): 30% continuous assessment + 70% exam]*

So the assignments and your tests, they matter, but the exam at the end really decides a lot of things. And that's why most of us who school in Nigeria tend to prepare for that big exam day.

### Here, the work is spread out

But here, it is different. Work is spread across the whole semester. So instead of the grade relying heavily on the exam, the course might be graded on a project, an essay, a presentation or group work, and that can literally be most of your grade. Or even all of it. Group work is such a common thing here, at least in my programme.

And in my school, the lecturer lets you know how you'll be assessed before the course even really starts. In the first class, the lecturer walks you through the course programme, how you're going to be assessed and all of that. So you really have to start working from week one. Because by the final weeks, which are the exam weeks, most of your grade is already decided.

### Nobody checks if you did the reading

And then there's something called independent study. In Estonia, one credit is 26 hours of your work, and most of those hours are not in a classroom. They are on you. So nobody checks if you did the reading. You just find out yourself. It shows in the way you understand the course, the way you discuss, and all of that.

*[on screen: 1 ECTS credit in Estonia = 26 hours of work]*

### If you fail or miss an exam

What happens when you fail or miss an exam is also different. In a lot of Nigerian universities, if you fail a course, it becomes a carryover. So you register for it again and write it in a later session.

At Tallinn University, where I'm schooling, a main exam is usually given two dates, plus one retake date. You register for the exam yourself. And if you register and you don't show up, and you didn't cancel, you're marked "non-appeared", and you lose one attempt. If you fail the main exam, you can retake it once, on the retake date. And if you still don't pass, you just have to take the whole course again.

*[on screen: Tallinn University: 2 exam dates + 1 retake. Cancel at least 24 hours before.]*

So if you can't make it for an exam, cancel your registration before the deadline, which is 24 hours before the exam, so you don't lose that attempt.

### Close

At least that's how it is in my programme. Did your exams ever let you use your phone? Tell me in the comments.

Honestly, I wouldn't even call it an exam in the Nigerian sense. We were allowed to use our phone, our laptop, the internet, even ChatGPT.

Imagine you're in Nigeria and you're caught with your phone in an exam. Expulsion. Carry-over at the minimum.

But it works here because the questions are not asking you to reproduce information. They're not asking you to memorise a definition and write it back. They're asking you to apply knowledge to a problem. So even if you Google the concept, if you don't understand it well enough to use it, having your phone wouldn't help you. And honestly, I think it's harder in some way, because you cannot just cram the night before.

At least that's how it is in my program. Did your exams ever let you use your phone?

script:
### Open

In Nigeria, lecturers are authority figures, full stop, and in Estonia I'm meant to call mine by his first name.

At home, you don't call your lecturers by their first name. You address them as Doctor, Professor, Sir, Ma. There's a very clear hierarchy.

So once, in class, my lecturer was talking to me and I said, Sir. And he was like, oh my God.

Here you just call your lecturers by their first name, and I'm like, what do you mean I should call you by your name? Are we mates?

### Respect shows up in different ways

I think the lecturer-student relationship is reasonably different between Nigeria and Europe. Respect shows up in different ways. The way you respect your lecturers or your professors in Nigeria is very different from the way respect is done here. Here in Estonia, everyone is on a first-name basis, and that includes your lecturers.

It's not that they are less respected. I genuinely respect my lecturers here. Respect is just expressed differently, through engagement, through asking questions, even pushing back. In Nigeria, the point is to absorb. Here, the point is to engage.

### The classroom

You see it in the classroom too. In a lot of Nigerian universities, especially in the big general courses, classes can be very large, and the lecturer does most of the talking. You listen, you take notes, and you read those notes for the exam. Here, as far as I can see, the classes are smaller, and you're also expected to participate.

### What respect looks like here

I think the respect we're raised with still works here. It just shows in a different way. For example, being respectful to your lecturer here might look like being prepared, keeping your deadlines and all of that. Starting your work early, asking for help. You can ask for help. You can really ask for help.

### The rules go both ways

And there are standards on the side of the lecturers too. For example, lecturers have seven days to put exam results in the system, or ten days if more than 50 students registered. When your results come out, you can get feedback. In fact, you can even contest your grade if you have enough evidence, and you have 10 working days to do that. So you don't have to anticipate or guess. Things are standardised on both sides, the student side and the lecturer side.

*[on screen: Tallinn University: results within 7 days (10 if more than 50 students registered). Contest a result within 10 working days.]*

### Don't throw away what Nigeria gave you

So if you studied in Nigeria and you're moving to Europe to study, you already have a lot of advantages that you're bringing in from Nigeria. Don't treat your education from Nigeria as something you just forget about. I promise you, it's gonna help you if you know how to use it well.

### Close

Did you call your lecturers Sir or Ma? Tell me in the comments.
